claims.text: A framework coupling high-throughput CALPHAD modeling, machine-learning corrections, and targeted experiments can accurately and efficiently predict liquidus and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family.
The targeted properties include melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change on melting, and other liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
HEAs typically exhibit high configurational entropy and simple BCC or FCC structures.
The framework can be applied to as-cast or homogenized single-phase HEAs and to well-characterized multiphase HEAs.
High-throughput CALPHAD calculations can be combined with selective experimental validation to refine thermodynamic predictions.
Machine-learning correction factors can augment CALPHAD calculations in this framework.
Selective DSC, DTA, and high-temperature XRD measurements can refine the framework's predictions.
The applicable compositional range typically consists of equiatomic or near-equiatomic mixtures containing at least five principal elements.
Near-equilibrium measurements under controlled thermal conditions are appropriate for evaluating the proposed predictions.
Local atomic configurations and short-range order affect mixing enthalpy, entropy contributions, and atomic-size effects.
Local atomic configurations and short-range order mediate liquid-phase thermodynamic behavior during melting.
Mixing enthalpy, configurational entropy, and volume effects can be combined with computational screening to estimate melting properties quantitatively.
Machine-learning corrections account for complex interactions not fully represented by current CALPHAD databases and thereby improve property predictions.
The framework will predict all specified melting properties within approximately 5–10% of high-resolution experimental measurements across diverse HEA compositions.
One-by-one experimental measurements and limited CALPHAD evaluations are too labor-intensive or inefficient to map the vast HEA compositional space.
The approach is most applicable when constituent elements and their interactions are well represented in existing thermodynamic databases.
Predictions may be less reliable for systems with strong electronic or magnetic effects, scarce calibration data, unexpected liquid ordering, or liquid-phase separation.
The framework is falsified if more than 30% of tested compositions show prediction errors greater than 10% relative to experiment.
